title: Cities Linked by a Big Common Divisor

concept.title: Instead of testing all pairs, join every number to the other multiples of each divisor larger than the threshold
body: There are cities numbered `1` to `n`. Two cities `a` and `b` are joined by a road if their **greatest common divisor is larger than a threshold `t`**. There are no other roads. For each question, are the cities `a` and `b` connected (directly or through other cities)? Testing all pairs of cities costs about `n^2 / 2` gcd computations, much too slow for `n = 50000`.

Look at it from the side of the divisors. If `gcd(a, b) = g > t`, then `g` divides both `a` and `b`. Conversely, if some number `d > t` divides both `a` and `b`, then `gcd(a, b) >= d > t`, so the cities are joined. So `a` and `b` are joined **exactly when they have a common divisor `d > t`**. For each `d` from `t + 1` to `n`, all the multiples of `d` (`d, 2d, 3d, ...`) are therefore joined to each other, and it is enough to **union them all with `d` itself** (or with each other in a chain). The number of unions is `n/(t+1) + n/(t+2) + ... + n/n`, about `n ln n`, at most about half a million for `n = 50000`.

This is the *harmonic sum* trick (as in the sieve of Eratosthenes): looping over the multiples of every number takes O(n log n) in total. If `t = 0`, every `d` from 1 joins all numbers, so everyone is connected. If `t >= n`, nobody is joined.

statement: There are `n` cities numbered 1 to `n`. Two cities `a` and `b` are directly connected by a road if `gcd(a, b) > t`. For each of `q` questions with two cities `a` and `b`, print `yes` if there is a way to get from `a` to `b` along roads (a city is connected to itself), and `no` otherwise.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, `t` and `q`: the number of cities (numbered 1 to n), the threshold and the number of questions.
Each of the next `q` lines has two cities `a` and `b`.

examples.note: Only the cities 3 and 6 share a divisor larger than 2 (the number 3): no, no, yes.

hints: Two cities are directly connected exactly when they have a common divisor larger than t.
For every d larger than t, join d with all its multiples up to n.
A question is answered by comparing the groups of the two cities.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, t, q = map(int, input().split())
qs = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]

# Your code here

explanation: Every number d above the threshold is joined with all its multiples; two cities are connected exactly when they end in the same group of the union-find.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n + q), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

parent = []
size = []

def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def union(a, b):
    a, b = find(a), find(b)
    if a == b:
        return False
    if size[a] < size[b]:
        a, b = b, a
    parent[b] = a
    size[a] += size[b]
    return True

n, t, q = map(int, input().split())
qs = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]

parent.extend(range(n + 1))
size.extend([1] * (n + 1))
for d in range(t + 1, n + 1):
    for multiple in range(2 * d, n + 1, d):
        union(d, multiple)
print("\n".join("yes" if find(a) == find(b) else "no" for a, b in qs))
